chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Marwak ibn Ubayd, from Nasheeth ibn Salih, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'It is from the understanding (fiqh) of the guest that he should not fast voluntarily except with the permission of his host; and from the obedience of the wife to her husband is that she should not fast voluntarily except with his permission and command; and from the correctness of the slave, his obedience, and his sincerity to his master is that he should not fast voluntarily except with the permission of his master and his command; and from the righteousness of the child is that he should not fast voluntarily except with the permission of his parents and their command; otherwise, the guest would be ignorant, the wife disobedient, the slave wicked and disobedient, and the child disloyal.'

key_terms.فِقْهِ الضَّيْفِ: Understanding of the guest (contextual knowledge of etiquette)

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a wife, guest, or child to fast voluntarily according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes a nuanced jurisprudential framework where voluntary fasting is not an absolute right but is contingent upon the rights of others (haqq al-ibah) such as the host, husband, master, or parents. Shia scholars emphasize that this condition applies specifically to fasting that does not involve a vow (nadhr) or obligatory makeup (qada), highlighting the balance between individual devotion and social/familial duties. The text further categorizes the failure to seek permission as a specific moral defect—ignorance for the guest, disobedience for the wife, wickedness for the slave, and filial impiety for the child—underscoring the holistic nature of piety in Shia tradition.
